reason: The blood sample and nephron preparation visibly match the first filtering stage.
expectation: Blood will be filtered into the nephron while blood cells remain in the vessels.

effect: The filter passed water and small solutes into the tubule while retaining blood cells and most proteins; the next stage is selective recovery.
reaction: The separation makes the first filtering step clear.
reason: The tubule transporters are positioned to recover selected substances from the filtered sample.
expectation: Useful dissolved substances will move from the tubule back toward the blood.

effect: The tubule transporters recovered glucose and other useful substances toward the blood; water recovery is the next visible stage.
reaction: The distinction between filtering and selective recovery is clear.
reason: The water-permeable tubule is shown returning water to nearby blood vessels.
expectation: Some water will move from the tubule back toward the blood, leaving a more concentrated remaining fluid.

effect: Water returned toward the blood while wastes remained in the tubule; the remaining fluid needs a drainage route.
reaction: The sequence clearly separates recovery from excretion.
reason: Urinary drainage connects the kidney's collecting passages to the ureter and bladder.
expectation: The remaining fluid will enter the urinary drainage route as urine.

effect: The remaining fluid now travels as urine to the bladder, completing the filtering and recovery goal. The urinary organs still need connecting to the body.
reaction: The sequence from filtration to drainage is straightforward.
reason: The kidney pair has a named ureter slot, and the ureters carry urine toward the bladder.
expectation: The ureters will attach to the kidneys, leaving the bladder connection to complete.

effect: The ureters are attached to the kidney pair; the bladder slot remains.
reaction: The named slot made the connection straightforward.
reason: The bladder is the remaining named fitting for the kidney pair.
expectation: The bladder will attach to the urinary organ assembly.

effect: The bladder is attached, completing the kidney-to-bladder organ assembly; it still needs connecting to the body.
reason: The remaining goal is to connect the urinary organs to the body.
expectation: The urinary organs will join the body and its circulation.

effect: The kidneys are now connected to circulation and the ureters lead to the bladder, completing both chapter goals.
reaction: The final connection brings the filtering sequence into the larger body model.

mostWorthwhile.text: Filtering the blood and then recovering useful substances made the distinction between filtration and selective recovery clear, especially that normally almost all filtered glucose is recovered.

leastWorthwhile.text: The separate ureter and bladder fittings were straightforward but repetitive after the urine-drainage sequence had already shown their route.

surprise.text: The explicit recovery of almost all filtered glucose clarified that useful small substances enter the filtrate too; filtration alone does not separate all useful material from waste.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, though the separate urinary drainage sequence and organ fittings partly duplicated the same route. The planned pictures also did not explain what drives filtration or water recovery.

continue.text: I would continue: connecting the kidney process to the body's circulation was useful, and I would be curious to see how later systems build on it.
